reference: median ground of the whole Sentinel-1 frame 7091 (descending, track 27); not a hand-picked site
adwr_note: ADWR value is its own published InSAR deformation raster (units inferred as metres) averaged over the same pixels. Sentinel-1 2017-2026 is the same satellite as ours (a consistency check); RADARSAT-2 2010-2026 is an independent sensor over a longer period.
rate_sigma_note: Combines the straight-line fit error with the larger of: half the descending-vs-ascending difference, or our difference from ADWR's own Sentinel-1 rate over the same pixels (reference choice).

nisar.scope: Average over the whole study box (not only the sinking area), from consecutive pairs; very noisy.
nisar.status_note: Provisional NISAR data; short record; rate not yet reliable.

caveats: Referenced to the median ground of the whole satellite frame; a few mm/yr of bias is possible.
Troposphere (water vapour) is not corrected; solid-earth tide and ionosphere are.
Uncertainty combines the straight-line fit error with the disagreement between descending and ascending satellite tracks; reference-site bias is not separately included.
Sinking does not by itself show who or what caused it.
source: Sentinel-1 OPERA DISP-S1 block-final granules, 6-month steps
sign_convention: Positive values mean the ground moved toward the satellite; negative values mean it moved away (sinking). Measured along the satellite's slanted view, not straight down. (OPERA product convention.)
data_release: OPERA L3 DISP-S1 v1.0 (Sentinel-1), records 2016-07-16 to 2026-02-06

insights.summary: Over about 10 years, the ground in the sinking part of this area has dropped by roughly 10 cm (4 inches) on average, and the fastest spots have dropped more.

points.heading: What we found
points.text: About 85 square kilometres (33 square miles) of ground here is sinking at roughly 1.3 cm a year (0.5 inches a year), give or take 0.4 cm a year. In the fastest-sinking 5% of this patch, the ground drops by more than 2.0 cm a year.

points.heading: How sure are we?
points.text: Satellite views from two opposite directions both see the ground sinking here. Arizona's water agency (ADWR) also lists this area as an official sinking-ground zone, which it calls Picacho. But the match with ADWR's separate satellite is weak here. The sinking is small compared with the measurement error, so treat the exact speed as a rough estimate. Confidence that the ground is sinking here: medium. Confidence in the exact speed: low.

points.heading: Why is the ground sinking?
points.text: In farming valleys, the usual cause of sinking is groundwater being pumped out faster than rain and rivers refill it. When the water level drops, layers of clay and sand underground squeeze together and the land above settles. Irrigated farmland surrounds this area. Our data show where the ground is moving, not who is pumping or why. That needs other evidence.

points.heading: Why it matters
points.text: Sinking ground can crack roads, canals and wells, and can open long cracks in the ground called earth fissures. Much of the squeeze underground is permanent, so the space that once held water is lost for good.

points.heading: What about NASA's new satellite?
points.text: NASA's new NISAR satellite has watched this area for under four months. That is still too short, and too uncertain, to give a trustworthy speed, so the ten-year trend above comes from the older Sentinel-1 satellite. If NISAR keeps observing, we estimate it can confirm a speed here around September 2027.

points.heading: Good to know
points.text: These numbers are measured along the satellite's slanted view, not straight down, and relative to the surrounding ground. If the ground is moving straight down, the true drop is likely somewhat larger. All numbers are preliminary.
